source_text: ἀληθινοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ πνεύματος λεγόμενον παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ τὴν οἰκείωσιν τῆς φύσεως δηλοῖ: ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων πάντων τὸ αὐτῷ κατὰ δεσποτείαν ἢ πίστιν διαφέρειν· ὡς καὶ ἡμεῖς εἰώθαμεν λέγειν ἐπὶ μὲν τῶν ὁμοουσίων ἡμῖν «ὁ υἱός μου, τὸ πνεῦμά μου», ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν ἄλλων· «ὁ ἀγρός μου, ὁ ἵππος μου», ἀλλὰ καὶ «ὁ θεός μου». 2.35 ὃν τρόπον γὰρ τὸν τῆς θείας φύσεως ἐνυπόστατον λόγον οὐ τὸ ἁπλῶς καὶ 45 ἀπολελυμένως εἰρῆσθαι υἱὸν καὶ μονογενῆ καὶ λόγον τοῦ θεοῦ Χριστὸν δείκνυσιν γεγεννῆσθαι ἐκ τῆς ὑποστάσεως τοῦ θεοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἔχειν συνημμένην τὴν συλλαβὴν τοῦ «μοῦ» καὶ «σοῦ». 2.36 ὡς ἡνίκα ὁ μὲν θεὸς λέγῃ· «οὗτός ἐστιν ὁ υἱός μου ὁ ἀγαπητός·» καὶ πάλιν· «ὁ λόγος μου ὁ ἀγαθός·» καί· «ἡτοίμασα λύχνον τῷ Χριστῷ μου·» ἡμεῖς δὲ ἀνευφημοῦμεν· «ὁ υἱός σου, ὁ μονογενής σου, ὁ Χριστός σου». 2.37 οὐδέ γε μὴν τὸ ὁμωνύμως ἢ συνωνύμως περὶ ἡμῶν γεγράφθαι· «υἱοὶ ἀνθρώπων, ἕως πότε βαρυκάρδιοι;» ἐξέλκει τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ θεοῦ τῇ ὁμωνυμίᾳ τῆς θεότητος· οὕτω τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα οὐ τὸ ἁπλῶς εἰρῆσθαι «πνεῦμα», ἀλλὰ τὸ συνῆφθαι τῷ ὀνόματι ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ τὸ «μοῦ» ἢ ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς κτίσεως τὸ «σοῦ» ἢ καὶ τὴν «ἅγιος» ἢ «ἄφθαρτος» ἢ «αἰώνιος» λέξιν δηλοῖ ἐκπεπορεῦσθαι αὐτὸ ἐκ τῆς πατρικῆς ὑποστάσεως· οὐδέ γε μὴν τὸ ὁμωνύμως εἰρῆσθαι τὰ λειτουργικὰ καὶ τὰ ἡμῶν πνεύματα ἢ ἅγια ἢ αἰώνια ἐξέλκει αὐτὸ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν εἶναι ἀληθινὸν πνεῦμα τοῦ θεοῦ. 2.38 καὶ ἐν τοῖς αἰνίγμασιν γὰρ αὐτοῖς τοῖς περὶ αὐτοῦ εὑρίσκεταί τις πάντως δήλωσις περὶ τῆς θείας αὐτοῦ φύσεως καὶ δυνάμεως. τὰ δὲ κτίσματα πρὸς τὴν ἑαυτῶν φύσιν ἔλαβεν τὸ ἅγιον καὶ αἰώνιον, οὐ καθάπαξ ταῦτα κατὰ φύσιν ἐξ ἑαυτῶν ἔχοντα. 2.39 ἐπεὶ μή γε αὐτοὶ οὗτοι αἱρετικοὶ εὑρίσκονται κατηγοροῦντες ἑαυτῶν, ὅτι τὸ «μοῦ» ἐπὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ τὸ «ἅγιον» καὶ τὸ «αἰώνιον» ἁπλῶς δέχονται ὡς ἀγγέλλον ταυτότητα τῆς θεϊκῆς φύσεως; ἔπειτα πρὸς τούτοις οὐ τὴν ψύχωσιν ἡμῶν πνεῦμα ὠνόμασεν ἐν ταῖς προκειμέναις ἀποδείξεσιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ αὐτοῦ ἅγιον πνεῦμα. 2.40 ἐχόντων γὰρ ἡμῶν τὸ ἴδιον πνεῦμα ἐδόθη ἡμῖν καὶ τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ. εἶπεν γὰρ ὁ πατήρ· «οὐ μὴ καταμείνῃ τὸ πνεῦμά μου ἐν τοῖς ἀνθρώποις τούτοις,» καὶ ὁ υἱὸς· «λάβετε πνεῦμα ἅγιον.» δῆλον δέ, ὡς τοῖς ἤδη ἔχουσιν τὸ οἰκεῖον ἡμῶν πνεῦμα ἐλέγετο περὶ τοῦ θεϊκοῦ πνεύματος. 2.41 καθὰ τοίνυν ὁ υἱὸς λόγος τοῦ θεοῦ υἱικῶς γεννητικός· οὕτω τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα πνευματικῶς ἐκπορευτικὸν καὶ οὐ δημιουργικῶς. καὶ ὡς οὐδεμία παραλλαγὴ οὐσίας καὶ δυνάμεως καὶ δόξης τῷ μονογενεῖ υἱῷ πρὸς τὸν θεὸν πατέρα, διαφορὰ δὲ πᾶσα, εἴ γε θέμις τοῦτο φάναι, πρὸς τὴν κτίσιν· οὕτω καὶ τῷ ἑνὶ θεϊκῷ πνεύματι. 2.42 τὸ οὖν μηδὲ ἀκούειν τὰ αἱρετικῶν τοῦ μὴ καὶ προσιέμενον αὐτὰ ἀκούειν δικαιότερον. 3.ν Περὶ τοῦ ἐκ διαφόρων ὀνομάτων σημαίνεσθαι τὴν θεϊκὴν φύσιν τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος. 3.1 ὃ δὲ ἐλέγομεν ἐξ ἀρχῆς, δεύτερον μαρτυροῦσιν τὰ λόγια, ὅτι διάφορα θεοπρεπῆ ὀνόματά ἐστιν τῷ πνεύματι τοῦ θεοῦ πολλήν τε ἄλλην ἔμφασιν ἐπηρμένην καὶ σχέσιν ὑπερτέραν πάντων, καὶ τῷ πατρὶ καὶ τῷ υἱῷ συνεχῆ καὶ κρείττονα τῆς πρεπωδεστάτης ἑρμηνείας συνεισφέροντα τοῖς προκειμένοις θεωρήμασι· 3.2 καὶ ἔτι ἀναπλοῦντα ἔνια μὲν τὴν θεϊκὴν αὐτοῦ φύσιν ἔνια δὲ τὴν αὐθεντικὴν δύναμιν, καὶ παραμυθούμενα τὴν ἀδυναμίαν ἡμῶν τὴν περὶ τὸ ἀξίως ἐφικέσθαι αὐτοῦ ἢ ἑρμηνείᾳ ῥημάτων ἢ θεωρίᾳ νοῦ, καὶ παρρησίαν παρέχοντα ἀκινδύνως ὁμοούσιον τοῦ θεοῦ καλεῖν αὐτὸ καὶ πιστεύειν τῷ ἁγιασμῷ αὐτοῦ. 3.3 καὶ οὐχ εὑρίσκομεν οὐδὲν τῶν ἄλλων πνευμάτων καταξιωθὲν κληθῆναι τοῖς ὀνόμασι τούτοις· τὸ δὲ μόνως καὶ φύσει ὑπάρχον ταῦτα οὐδέν ἐστι τῶν πάντων, ἀλλὰ θεός. 3.4 ἔστιν δὲ τὰ ὀνόματα τάδε· πνεῦμα ἅγιον, ὡς πανταχοῦ γέγραπται· πνεῦμα ἁγιοσύνης, καὶ ἁγιάζον, ὡς γράφει Ῥωμαίοις «Παῦλος, δοῦλος Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ, κλητὸς ἀπόστολος ἀφωρισμένος εἰς εὐαγγέλιον θεοῦ, ὃ προεπηγγείλατο διὰ τῶν προφητῶν αὐτοῦ ἐν γραφαῖς ἁγίαις περὶ τοῦ υἱοῦ αὐτοῦ τοῦ γενομένου ἐκ σπέρματος ∆αυὶδ κατὰ σάρκα, τοῦ ὁρισθέντος υἱοῦ θεοῦ ἐν δυνάμει κατὰ πνεῦμα ἁγιοσύνης,» 3.5 καὶ πάλιν· «ἵνα γένηται ἡ προσφορὰ τῶν ἐθνῶν εὐπρόσδεκτος, 46 ἡγιασμένη ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ», καὶ ἑτέρωθι· «ἡμεῖς δὲ ὀφείλομεν εὐχαριστεῖν τῷ θεῷ πάντοτε περὶ ὑμῶν, ἀδελφοὶ ἠγαπημένοι ὑπὸ κυρίου, ὅτι εἵλετο ὑμᾶς ὁ θεὸς ἀπαρχὴν εἰς σωτηρίαν ἐν ἁγιασ μῷ πνεύματος καὶ πίστει ἀληθείας.» 3.6 πνεῦμα δυνάμεως καὶ ἀγάπης καὶ σωφρονισμοῦ, ὡς Παῦλος ἐν δευτέρᾳ ἐπιστολῇ πρὸς
pass_a_gloss: [...] of the true Son and the true Spirit, being said by God, makes clear the kinship of the nature; but in the case of all the others, the belonging to him by lordship or faith; as we too are accustomed to say, in the case of those of the same essence with us, 'my son, my spirit', but in the case of the others: 'my field, my horse', but also 'my God'. 2.35 For in the way that, as to the subsisting Word of the divine nature, it is not the having been called simply and absolutely Son and only-begotten and Word of God, Christ, that shows him to have been begotten out of the hypostasis of God, but the having the syllable of the 'my' and 'your' joined on. 2.36 As whenever God says: 'this is my Son, the beloved'; and again: 'my Word, the good'; and: 'I prepared a lamp for my Christ'; and we acclaim in return: 'your Son, your only-begotten, your Christ'. 2.37 Nor indeed does the having been written about us with the same name or a like name: 'sons of men, until when heavy-hearted?' drag away the Son of God from the Godhead by the sameness of name; thus as to the Holy Spirit, not the having been called simply 'spirit', but the having joined to the name either, as from God, the 'my', or, as from the creation, the 'your', or also the word 'holy' or 'incorruptible' or 'everlasting', makes clear that it has proceeded out of the paternal hypostasis; nor indeed does the having been called by the same name, either holy or everlasting, the ministering spirits and ours drag it away from being by nature true spirit of God. 2.38 For also in the riddles themselves about it there is found by someone wholly some declaration about its divine nature and power. But the created things received the holy and everlasting toward their own nature, not at all having these things by nature from themselves. 2.39 Since otherwise are not these heretics themselves found accusing themselves, that they simply accept the 'my' in the case of the Son of God and the 'holy' and the 'everlasting' as announcing sameness of the divine nature? Then besides these things, it was not our ensoulment that he named spirit in the proofs set before, but his own Holy Spirit. 2.40 For while we had our own spirit there was given to us also that of God. For the Father said: 'my spirit shall by no means remain in these men', and the Son: 'receive Holy Spirit'. And it is clear that to those already having our own spirit it was being said about the divine spirit. 2.41 Accordingly, as the Son, Word of God, [is] son-wise of begetting; so the Holy Spirit spirit-wise of proceeding and not creatively. And as [there is] no variation of essence and power and glory for the only-begotten Son toward God the Father, but every difference, if indeed it is right to say this, toward the creation; so also for the one divine spirit. 2.42 So the not even hearing the things of heretics [is] more just than the hearing them, not also admitting them. 3.ν [Chapter title:] On the divine nature of the Holy Spirit being signified from different names. 3.1 And what we were saying from the beginning, the oracles testify secondly, that there are different God-befitting names for the spirit of God, and contributing to the propositions set before much other lifted-up significance and a relation higher than all, and continuous with the Father and the Son and stronger than the most fitting interpretation; 3.2 and further unfolding, some, its divine nature, and some its sovereign power, and consoling our weakness about attaining it worthily either by interpretation of words or by contemplation of mind, and providing boldness without danger to call it of the same essence as God and to trust in its sanctification. 3.3 And we find none of the other spirits deemed worthy to be called by these names; but that which alone and by nature is these things is nothing of all things, but God. 3.4 And the names are these: Holy Spirit, as is written everywhere; spirit of holiness, and sanctifying, as Paul writes to Romans: 'Paul, slave of Jesus Christ, called apostle, set apart into the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in holy writings about his Son, the one who came of the seed of David according to flesh, the one marked out Son of God in power according to spirit of holiness', 3.5 and again: 'so that the offering of the nations become well-acceptable, sanctified in Holy Spirit', and elsewhere: 'but we ought to give thanks to God always about you, brothers loved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruit into salvation in sanctification of spirit and faith of truth'. 3.6 Spirit of power and love and self-control, as Paul in the second letter to [...]
pass_b_english: … true Son and the true Spirit, when God says it, shows that they are akin to him in nature; but of all the others it shows that they belong to him by lordship or by faith. So we too are used to saying, of those who share our essence, “my son, my spirit”, but of other things, “my field, my horse”, and also “my God”.

For in the same way, it is not his being called simply and without qualification Son, and Only-begotten, and Word of God, and Christ, that shows that the Word of the divine nature, who subsists in his own right, was begotten from the hypostasis of God; it is his having the syllable “my” or “your” joined to these names. So when God says, “This is my beloved Son” (Matthew 3:17), and again, “My good word” (Psalm 45:1), and, “I have prepared a lamp for my Christ” (Psalm 132:17), we in turn acclaim him: “Your Son, your Only-begotten, your Christ.”

Nor, indeed, does the fact that Scripture writes of us with the same or a like name, “Sons of men, how long will you be heavy of heart?” (Psalm 4:2), drag the Son of God away from the Godhead by the sharing of a name. So with the Holy Spirit: it is not his being called simply “spirit”, but the joining to the name of “my”, as from God, or of “your”, as from creation, or of the word “holy” or “incorruptible” or “everlasting”, that shows that he has proceeded from the Father’s hypostasis. Nor, indeed, does the fact that the ministering spirits and our own spirits are called by the same name, “holy” or “everlasting”, drag him away from being by nature the true Spirit of God.

For even in the riddles that speak of him there is always some declaration of his divine nature and power. But created things received holiness and everlastingness in the measure of their own nature, and do not possess these things by nature of themselves at all.

Otherwise, are these heretics not found accusing themselves, since they readily accept the “my” said of the Son of God, and the “holy” and the “everlasting”, as announcing that he has the same divine nature? Then, besides this, in the proofs set out above it was not the life of our souls that he named “spirit”, but his own Holy Spirit. For when we already had our own spirit, the Spirit of God was given us as well. The Father said, “My spirit shall not remain in these men” (Genesis 6:3), and the Son, “Receive the Holy Spirit” (John 20:22). And it is clear that it was to those who already had our own spirit that these words about the divine Spirit were spoken.

As the Son, then, the Word of God, is begotten as a son, so the Holy Spirit proceeds as spirit, and not by way of creation. And as there is no variation of essence, power or glory between the only-begotten Son and God the Father, but every difference, if it is right to say so, between him and creation, so it is with the one divine Spirit as well.
So it is more just not even to listen to what heretics say than to listen to it, even without accepting it.
That the divine nature of the Holy Spirit is shown by various names.

As we said at the beginning, the oracles bear witness, in the second place, that the Spirit of God has various names fit for God. To the propositions before us these names bring much further, exalted meaning, and a relation that is above all things, bound closely to the Father and the Son, and beyond the most fitting expression. They unfold, some of them, his divine nature, and others his sovereign power. They console our weakness in reaching him worthily, whether in the expression of words or in the contemplation of the mind. And they give us boldness to call him, without danger, consubstantial with God, and to trust in his sanctification.
We do not find any of the other spirits deemed worthy to be called by these names; and that which alone and by nature is all these things is no one among all things, but God.

These are the names. Holy Spirit, as is written everywhere. Spirit of holiness, and sanctifying, as Paul writes to the Romans: “Paul, a servant of Jesus Christ, called to be an apostle, set apart for the gospel of God, which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures concerning his Son, who was born of the seed of David according to the flesh, who was declared Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness” (Romans 1:1-4). And again: “That the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 15:16). And elsewhere: “But we ought always to give thanks to God for you, brothers beloved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits for salvation in sanctification of the Spirit and faith in the truth” (2 Thessalonians 2:13).

choices.issue: Old draft garbled, abbreviated and unparagraphed
choices.choice: Retranslated the whole section from the Greek. The old English turned 2.34 into 'it differs by lordship or by faith' (διαφέρειν here: belongs to him); made 2.35 say the Word was 'shown to have become Son'; read ἐξέλκει (drags away) as 'bring forth' in 2.37, reversing the sense; garbled 2.40 ('It is clear. And, as it was said concerning the divine Spirit, that it is like our own indwelling Spirit'); rendered υἱικῶς as 'paternally'; turned 2.42 into 'and to approach listening to these things'; ran the chapter title 3.ν into the prose; missed 'in the second place' in 3.1 (the counterpart of 'First' in 2.1); and rendered ἀναπλοῦντα (unfolding) as 'replenishing' in 3.2. References: 'Matt 3:17', 'Rom 1:1-4', 'Rom 15:16' written in full; 'cf. Genesis 6:3' made Genesis 6:3; Psalm 45:1 and Psalm 132:17 added; Psalm 4:2, John 20:22, 2 Thessalonians 2:13 kept.

choices.term: ἀληθινοῦ υἱοῦ καὶ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ πνεύματος λεγόμενον
choices.english: … true Son and the true Spirit, when God says it
choices.why: The section opens mid-sentence; the previous section ends “So the “my”, said of the …”. Only this section's words are translated.

choices.term: τὸ αὐτῷ κατὰ δεσποτείαν ἢ πίστιν διαφέρειν
choices.english: that they belong to him by lordship or by faith
choices.why: διαφέρει with the dative means 'belongs to'; the old 'it differs' missed the contrast with kinship of nature.
Didymus' short form of the Greek Psalm 44:2 (“my heart has poured out a good word”), English Psalm 45:1, which the KJV renders “a good matter”; he reads it of the Word.

choices.term: ἐξέλκει … τῆς θεότητος / τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν εἶναι
choices.english: drag … away from the Godhead / from being by nature
choices.why: ἐξέλκω with the genitive: to drag away from. A shared name does not remove the Son or the Spirit from the divine nature.
καθάπαξ with a negative strengthens it: creatures do not have holiness of themselves in any way.
Rhetorical question: the Spirit-fighters accept the same words as proof of the Son's divinity, so they condemn themselves.

choices.english: is begotten as a son … proceeds as spirit
choices.why: The active-looking adjectives describe the manner of origin of Son and Spirit, not their power to beget; read in the sense of γεννητός. Recorded under problems.

choices.term: τὸ οὖν μηδὲ ἀκούειν … τοῦ μὴ καὶ προσιέμενον αὐτὰ ἀκούειν δικαιότερον
choices.english: it is more just not even to listen to what heretics say than to listen to it, even without accepting it
choices.why: Comparative genitive with a negated participle: not hearing is better than hearing without consent. The line is compressed; see problems.

choices.term: 3.ν Περὶ τοῦ ἐκ διαφόρων ὀνομάτων σημαίνεσθαι
choices.english: That the divine nature of the Holy Spirit is shown by various names.
choices.why: Chapter title set as its own short paragraph.

choices.english: the oracles bear witness, in the second place
choices.why: Answers 'First' in 2.1: the second heading of the Scripture proofs.

choices.term: πολλήν τε ἄλλην ἔμφασιν ἐπηρμένην καὶ σχέσιν ὑπερτέραν πάντων … συνεισφέροντα
choices.english: To the propositions before us these names bring much further, exalted meaning, and a relation that is above all things …
choices.why: The long participial period (3.1-3.2) is broken into four English sentences, keeping each participle as its own verb.

choices.term: τὸ δὲ μόνως καὶ φύσει ὑπάρχον ταῦτα οὐδέν ἐστι τῶν πάντων, ἀλλὰ θεός
choices.english: that which alone and by nature is all these things is no one among all things, but God
choices.why: 'All things' is the created universe; the Spirit is not one item in it.
'45' and '46' are printed page numbers in the copy-text; skipped. Split word ἁγιασ μῷ read as one word.
